title: Trump Fires NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox, Leaving Board Without Quorum
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox, a Democrat appointed by Joe Biden. The five-member board already had two vacancies, so her removal left it without the three members needed to issue decisions. Wilcox called the firing unlawful and said she would challenge it. Trump did not fire the entire board.
description_long: President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox late on January 27, 2025. The board, which adjudicates disputes under federal labor law and protects workers’ rights to organize, had already been operating with two vacancies. Removing Wilcox left only two sitting members, below the three-member quorum required for the NLRB to issue decisions in cases. The agency could continue some work through its regional offices, but the board could not decide routine complaints alleging that employers or unions had violated labor law. Wilcox said her dismissal was illegal and that she would pursue legal challenges. The president’s authority to remove NLRB members is disputed because federal law provides for removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance. The dispute became part of a broader legal fight over presidential control of independent agencies. This was a firing of one member that eliminated the board’s quorum, not a dismissal of every NLRB member.

corrected_wording.label: Title and scope correction
corrected_wording.text: Trump fired one NLRB member, Gwynne Wilcox. Two vacancies already existed; her removal eliminated the quorum. The source does not support “entire board.”

source_access_notes: Search retrieved the supplied Reuters report and its details on Wilcox, existing vacancies, loss of quorum, and her response.
rationale: Corrects the false entire-board claim, explains the quorum effect, and attributes the legal dispute rather than asserting the firing was definitively unlawful.

corrected_wording.label: Title correction
corrected_wording.text: The assigned NYT source concerns Trump’s New York conviction and does not identify any pardoned New Jersey politicians. Do not state the alleged pardons as fact without named recipients and clemency records.

source_access_notes: The linked NYT story is unrelated. Focused search of DOJ’s clemency list and news results did not identify the alleged New Jersey beneficiaries or matching pardon event.

title: Education Department Directs Schools to End Racial Preferences
description_medium: On February 15, 2025, the Education Department directed schools and colleges receiving federal funds to end the use of racial preferences and stereotypes in programs and activities. The department said institutions that failed to comply could face investigations and loss of federal funding. This was agency guidance applying federal civil-rights law, not a March executive order abolishing DEI programs across public education.
description_long: The Education Department issued guidance on February 15, 2025, directing schools and colleges that receive federal funding to end programs and activities the department viewed as using racial preferences or stereotypes. The guidance interpreted Title VI, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin in federally funded programs. The department warned that institutions that failed to comply could face investigation and loss of federal funds. The move followed President Donald Trump’s January executive order ending DEI programs in the federal government, but it was a separate Education Department action directed at schools and universities. It did not itself terminate every diversity program nationwide; instead, it announced the administration’s enforcement position and set a short compliance period for institutions. Critics said the guidance could chill lawful efforts to address discrimination, while department officials described it as enforcing civil-rights protections.

corrected_wording.label: Title, date, and action correction
corrected_wording.text: The school guidance was issued by the Education Department on February 15, 2025; it was not the March executive order described in the packet. Avoid saying all DEI programs were terminated.

source_access_notes: Used the Education Department’s same-event February 15 release; supplied NBC page concerns a separate order to dismantle the department.
rationale: Separates the February school guidance from the unrelated March department-dismantling order and describes what the guidance directed rather than claiming universal implementation.

title: House Passes Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill by a 215–214 Vote
description_medium: The House passed President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill on May 22, 2025, by a 215–214 vote, sending the reconciliation measure to the Senate. The package combined tax cuts with major changes to Medicaid and food assistance. The Congressional Budget Office warned that the bill would add trillions of dollars to federal debt over a decade, while the health-program changes were projected to reduce coverage.
description_long: The House of Representatives narrowly passed H.R. 1, President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, on May 22, 2025. The vote was 215 to 214, after an overnight debate and a lengthy effort by Republican leaders to secure enough support. The reconciliation measure combined tax provisions with spending and policy changes, including reductions to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. It also raised the federal debt limit. The bill then moved to the Senate, where lawmakers could revise it before final passage. Congressional budget analysts warned that the legislation would increase federal deficits and leave millions fewer people with health coverage than under current law. Specific cost and coverage estimates depended on the version of the bill and assumptions used. The vote was a consequential step in advancing Trump’s domestic agenda, but House passage did not make the bill law or settle its final details.

corrected_wording.label: Figure correction
corrected_wording.text: The House vote was 215–214. The supplied Medicaid and SNAP dollar amounts are corrupted; use a version-specific CBO score before adding them.

source_access_notes: Search located Reuters’ same-day coverage, House vote details, and CBO’s version-specific House-passed Medicaid estimate.
rationale: Retains the passage event, replaces corrupted amounts with version-specific cautious wording, and distinguishes House passage from enactment.
